catalog_quote: Within the domain of the word, stress and pitch are combined to form three degrees of accent - primary or strong (1), secondary (2) and tertiary or weak (3). In words containing only short vowels, the accent pattern is straightforward, adhering to the following basic design: 1 3 2 3 2 3 ... Now when a long vowel occurs in an even syllable, the basic pattern may not be adhered to ... If it is, then the stronger accent on the syllable, preceding it, will be attracted onto it. ... In disyllabic words with a long vowel in the second syllable, the accent is optionally deflected to the second syllable, providing the possible pattern 3 1. However, if the long vowel is a high one, it may be broken, producing a pattern 1 3 2. ... sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same chapter (Jacobs 2000, re-issued 2003 with a second DOI): 'The revenge of the uneven trochee' is an OT analysis of Latin main stress and shortening/syncope; I obtained the publisher's-version PDF (Radboud Repository hdl 2066/104107, green OA per Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar; the repository itself could not be reached by automated download, so it was downloaded from the 2019 Internet Archive copy; 21 pp., full text layer) and it contains no mention of Yindjibarndi, any Australian language, Wordick or Pama-Nyungan. Glottolog's attachment of ids 450864/453625 to yind1247 is a mis-tag; both items are irrelevant (other language: Latin), silent on the catalog, priority none. No new first-hand stress source for Yindjibarndi surfaced. The catalog's weight-hedged coding continues to rest on Wordick 1982 sec. 2.3.2 (pp. 41-42), which I re-read from the page image and on-disk text this search of works with stress in the title: initial primary accent with alternating secondaries (1 3 2 3 2 3), a long vowel in an even syllable optionally/ordinarily attracting the stronger accent when pronounced long, rules explicitly 'not hard and fast' -- consistent with the catalog. Blocked routes noted in : degruyterbrill (bot challenge), repository.ubn.ru.

new_statements.citation: Wordick, F.J.F. (1982). The Yindjibarndi Language. Pacific Linguistics Series C, No. 71. Canberra: ANU. sec. 2.3.2 Accent, printed pp. 41-42 (PDF pp. 55-56).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3.2 Accent, printed p. 41 (PDF p. 55), first four paragraphs; continued p. 42
new_statements.reading: Primary accent on the first syllable with secondary accents on following odd syllables (1 3 2 3 2 3) whenever all vowels are short or long vowels sit only in odd syllables; a long vowel in an even syllable, if pronounced long, pulls the stronger accent off the preceding syllable onto itself (disyllables with long V2 'optionally' 3 1; trisyllables with long aa in syllable 2 'ordinarily' 3 1 2; high long vowels are usually broken into two shorts and keep 1 3 2 3), and Wordick adds that 'these rules are not hard and fast'. That is a weight-sensitive (long-vowel-attracting) system whose weight effect is optional/variable, which is exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding. Stanton 2022 (already held by the project, sec. 5.2 ex. 58) is secondary and restates Wordick pp. 41-42.

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: default initial primary with alternating secondaries; a long vowel in the second syllable, if realised long, attracts primary, optionally in disyllables and 'ordinarily' with aa in trisyllables; high long vowels usually broken; final consonants weightless) rests on Wordick 1982 sec. 2.3.2, the sole reference grammar of the language, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated pages in the PDF we hold/text/page images. Glottolog's only other descriptive items are the two records of Stanton 2021/2022 (NLLT), downloaded now: it explicitly derives its stress/footing schema from Wordick pp. 41-42 and restates the system as weight-sensitive and variable with weightless consonants, confirming our reading including the 'hedged' (optional/variable) character. sources.quote: 'stress in Yindjibarndi is weight-sensitive and variable: a long vowel can be realized as a single unit or two distinct short vowels in hiatus.' Ex. (58) gives footings: CV:-CV ("CV:-CV) 1-0 or ("CV.V)(-CV) 10-2; CVCV:-CV either (CV."CV:)(-CV) 01-2 (peninitial long vowel takes primary) or ("CV.CV)(V-CV) 10-20 (broken vowel); CVCVCV-CV ("CV.CV)(CV-CV). Also: 'consonants do not carry a mora in Yindjibarndi'.
